newsitem.title: USA: Rubin seeks changes in U.S. Senate tax bill.
newsitem.headline: Rubin seeks changes in U.S. Senate tax bill.

text.p: Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, in a letter released on Thursday, expressed "very serious concerns" about tax proposals now under consideration in Congress.

In the letter sent to Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth on Wednesday, Rubin said the benefits of any tax cuts should be distributed equally to all income levels but that the Senate proposals did not appear to meet that target.

Treasury's analysis showed 65.5 percent of the estimated $85 billion proposed in tax cuts over five years, once fully in place, would go to the top 20 percent of taxpayers, Rubin said. Only 13 percent would go to the bottom 30 percent.
Among specific changes suggested by Rubin was a revision to allow moderate and low-income families to claim a child credit before the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) was applied.

"Otherwise, families who most need the help from a child credit would not be eligible," Rubin said, since millions of families owe taxes before the EITC is applied but not after and so would not get the extra benefit from the child credit.

Rubin also said a full 100 percent credit should be restored for students in their first two years of college education and additional tax relief provided to create incentives for life-long education.

Rubin also expressed concern about "the proliferation of IRA (Individual Retirement Account) relief and other tax-favored savings incentives without income limitations" contained among the Senate tax proposals. He said the more generous treatment might not lead to greater savings and would favor wealthier taxpayers.

Rubin said the Clinton administration did not favor indexing capital gains to reduce the amount of tax that investors would pay on gains resulting from inflation, noting that would specially favor the wealthy when applied in combination with lower tax rates on capital gains.
"Our preference would be to limit capital gains relief to sales of residences and small business investments," Rubin said.
